source.title: Mental health in Britain: understanding public attitudes across the Seven Segments (More in Common and Wellcome mental health report)
source.publisher: More in Common, commissioned by Wellcome
source.fieldwork: Quantitative: nationally representative online poll of GB adults, fieldwork 27 September - 8 October 2025, weighted to the GB adult population. Qualitative: 7 semi-structured focus groups (one per segment), December 2025 - January 2026.
source.sample: 4,071 GB adults (described in the front matter as 4,000)
source.segmentation: More in Common 2025 Seven Segments: Progressive Activists 12%, Incrementalist Left 21%, Established Liberals 9%, Sceptical Scrollers 10%, Rooted Patriots 20%, Traditional Conservatives 8%, Dissenting Disruptors 20% (p7-8)
source.page_numbering: Pages are PDF page indices (matching the '===== PAGE n =====' markers in the extracted text). The printed page number on each page is one lower.
source.extraction_notes: Every value is printed in the report text or as a data label on a chart. Several charts (Figures 2, 7, 9, 16, 17, 18) are unlabelled dot plots; findings from those are given as direction only with value null and no numbers read off the axis. 'Other 6 segments' comparisons are the report's own comparison group, not the national total.

findings.finding: Tied with Dissenting Disruptors for highest personal experience of a mental health issue; also highest for close friend and immediate family.
findings.value: self 40%, close friend 27%, immediate family 30% (all: 28/16/22)
findings.wording: Have you, or someone you know experienced a mental health issue? Select all that apply

findings.finding: Most comfortable segment if a friend opened up about mental illness.
findings.value: 86% comfortable (very 44, somewhat 42; not very 8, not at all 2)
findings.wording: How comfortable, if at all, would you feel if a friend shared how their mental illness affects their life?

findings.finding: Rarely frame mental health individually; see it as a structural problem driven by social media, work and the cost of living, and talk about it in institutional terms (waiting times, delays).
Want the government to do more on mental health, 11 points above the national average; much more likely than others to say 'much more'.
findings.value: 86% do more (national 75%); 53% 'much more' vs 37% other six segments
findings.wording: Do you think the government should be doing more or less to improve mental health support and services in Britain today?

findings.finding: Strongest belief that mental health should be treated as importantly as physical health, yet least likely to think parity exists today.
findings.value: 86% should be equal (other six segments 71%); 72% say it is treated as less important (national 55%)
findings.wording: Mental health should be treated with the same level of importance as physical health

findings.finding: Only segment as likely (or more) to back extra government research investment for mental health as for physical health; far more likely to strongly support mental health research investment.
findings.value: 59% strongly support vs 33% other six segments
findings.wording: To what extent would you support or oppose the government investing more to research better treatments for mental health conditions, such as anxiety or depression?

findings.finding: Above-average awareness of treatments from talking therapy to apps and more likely to think new treatments could work - except AI chatbots, which they are more sceptical of than any other segment.
More likely than others to think new scientific breakthroughs are needed for young people's mental health.
findings.value: 51% vs 41% other six segments
findings.wording: To tackle rising mental health problems in young people, we will need new scientific breakthroughs and methods

findings.finding: Fewer than a third think the quality and range of treatments has improved recently, in line with the public; pessimistic about government's ability or willingness to deliver, which can tip into futility without systemic service change.
findings.value: less than a third

findings.finding: Strongly trust people with lived experience, universities and the NHS; more trusting than other segments of charities, philanthropic and intergovernmental bodies; distinctly distrust big tech and pharmaceutical companies, seeing profit as conflicting with public interest.
findings.wording: To what extent, if at all, do you trust each of the following to provide accurate information about mental health to the public?

findings.finding: Exceptional lack of trust in pharmaceutical companies, on a par with Dissenting Disruptors.
Half get key information from social media; more likely to learn about science via podcasts and museums.
findings.value: social media about half (p27); podcasts 29% vs national 16% and museums/exhibitions 32% vs national 20% (p64)

findings.finding: Most likely segment to want mental health to feature more in culture and entertainment, especially TV and film storylines. The report prints two different figures.
findings.value: 37% want more (p51); 41% want more vs 28% public (p64)
findings.wording: Would you like mental health problems or solutions to feature more or less in culture and entertainment?

findings.finding: Most moved by the 'wider practical benefit' frame (new treatments cutting waits and easing NHS pressure) rather than lived experience or clinical evidence.
findings.wording: RCT split-sample on support for pharmaceutical treatment

findings.finding: Healthcare professionals or people with lived experience; channels TV/film, social media, books.

quotes.quote: I think (mental health) is a consequence of other problems. I think it's hard to separate them. I think they're connected.
quotes.speaker: Levi, tradesman, Progressive Activist

quotes.quote: I think the approach is effective. It's just whether the patient can access them.
quotes.speaker: Kira, Progressive Activist

quotes.quote: I think that the NHS is so stretched as it is and the problems that we're facing with mental health.
quotes.speaker: Kira, practice manager, Progressive Activist

findings.finding: Slightly below average personal experience; average for family.
findings.value: self 24%, close friend 18%, immediate family 22% (all: 28/16/22)
findings.wording: Have you, or someone you know experienced a mental health issue? Select all that apply

findings.finding: Highly comfortable if a friend opened up.
findings.value: 85% comfortable (very 42, somewhat 43; not very 9, not at all 2)
findings.wording: How comfortable, if at all, would you feel if a friend shared how their mental illness affects their life?

findings.finding: Highest share wanting the government to do more, but unlike Progressive Activists they have some faith the government can deliver.
findings.wording: Do you think the government should be doing more or less to improve mental health support and services in Britain today?

findings.finding: Like others they think services are in a bad state, but remain hopeful; more likely than average to approve of the government's handling and to think the range and quality of treatments have improved.
Strong belief in parity, but more likely than average to think parity already exists in Britain.
findings.value: 85% should be treated equally
findings.wording: Mental health should be treated with the same level of importance as physical health

findings.finding: Optimism comes from mental health finally getting attention, which they expect to bring investment and treatment breakthroughs.

High awareness of new interventions and often most likely to rate them effective and to feel comfortable using them personally, across drug, non-drug and digital routes; highest belief in digital treatments.
findings.value: 37% say digital treatments (AI chatbots, apps) have potential, highest segment, 6 points above average

findings.finding: Exceptionally high trust across many voices; prize lived experience most but also far more trusting than others of institutions such as universities, charities and the NHS (net trust above other six segments on every voice tested).
findings.wording: To what extent, if at all, do you trust each of the following to provide accurate information about mental health to the public? (net trust)

findings.finding: Want clarity on limits of treatments and dislike one-size-fits-all narratives; some worry medication is reached for too quickly before talking.
Reached through live TV and social media; biggest music fans and heavy podcast listeners.
findings.value: live TV 64%; social media 46%

findings.finding: Want more mental health in media and most likely to be moved by it.
findings.value: 34% want more (p51); 46% say seeing mental health content made the issue feel more important (p66)

findings.finding: Most moved by lived experience testimony (e.g. people saying medication helped them return to daily life).
findings.wording: RCT split-sample on support for pharmaceutical treatment

findings.finding: Healthcare professionals or people with lived experience; channels TV/film, social media, podcasts.

quotes.quote: For some people, medication is the right solution, but I think a lot of people maybe go on that too quickly without actually talking to someone.

findings.finding: Low personal experience; tied with Traditional Conservatives as least likely to have close friends or family with experience.
findings.value: self 16%, close friend 9%, immediate family 13% (all: 28/16/22)
findings.wording: Have you, or someone you know experienced a mental health issue? Select all that apply

findings.finding: Mostly comfortable, slightly below average.
findings.value: 74% comfortable (very 36, somewhat 38; not very 15, not at all 2)
findings.wording: How comfortable, if at all, would you feel if a friend shared how their mental illness affects their life?

findings.finding: Nearly twice as likely as the public to say the government handles mental health well; by far the most likely to think services are improving.
findings.value: 39% handling well (general public 20%; other six segments 18%)
findings.wording: The government is handling the issue of mental health well

findings.finding: More likely than others to say the range and quality of treatments has improved in recent years.
findings.value: range 46% vs 32%; quality 44% vs 31% (other six segments)
findings.wording: The range / quality of mental health treatments in the UK has improved in recent years

findings.finding: Medium-to-low salience: less likely than average to say government must do more, which the report links to their optimism rather than indifference.
Highly optimistic that science and technology will help.
findings.value: 77% say advances will help people lead better lives (public 65%); 37% say science has 'a great deal' of potential vs 30% other six segments
findings.wording: Science has 'a great deal' of potential to help people with mental health issues through new discoveries

findings.finding: Profit motive is no barrier: most likely segment to think pharma and tech firms can improve lives; only segment with net positive trust in pharmaceutical companies and tech companies on mental health, and uniquely trusting of national government.
findings.value: pharma potential 62%; tech potential 51%

findings.finding: Techno-optimists: highest openness to mobile apps, wearables and virtual reality for mental health.
Back early intervention on pragmatic grounds that prevention is more efficient than cure.
Welcome portrayals but plurality think the current amount is right; most likely to attend theatre and to want live performance to portray mental health.
findings.value: 27% want more; 48% right amount

findings.finding: Only segment for whom the clinical evidence frame alone significantly raised support; practical benefit second; lived experience less effective.
findings.wording: RCT split-sample on support for pharmaceutical treatment

findings.finding: Healthcare professionals; channels TV/film, social media.

quotes.quote: I think as a whole, support is improving.

quotes.quote: I'm a great believer in prevention, but we just don't have it anymore, do we? We're more of a reactive country.

quotes.quote: for companies at least large organisation, it's become like a checklist.

findings.finding: Third-highest personal experience, at the national average.
findings.value: self 28%, close friend 16%, immediate family 19% (all: 28/16/22)
findings.wording: Have you, or someone you know experienced a mental health issue? Select all that apply

findings.finding: Least comfortable segment, though still a majority.
findings.value: 55% comfortable (very 19, somewhat 36; don't know 12; not very 25, not at all 7)
findings.wording: How comfortable, if at all, would you feel if a friend shared how their mental illness affects their life?

findings.finding: Lowest confidence in science and innovation to help; few think treatments have improved or will improve.
findings.value: 64% say science has potential through discoveries (public 86%); 60% for mental health specifically (public 77%)
findings.wording: To what extent do you think science has the potential to help people, through new discoveries on treating mental health issues specifically?

findings.finding: Lowest net support of any segment for more research investment in both physical and mental health, with mental health lower than physical (chart unlabelled; direction only).
findings.wording: To what extent would you support or oppose the government investing more to research better treatments for... (net support)

findings.finding: See greater openness cynically as 'more talk, less action' without better services; linked to atomisation.
findings.value: 58% often feel disconnected from society (second only to Dissenting Disruptors)

findings.finding: Particularly cynical about pharmacological treatment.
findings.value: 53% say prescribed medication is effective; 33% ineffective
findings.wording: How effective or ineffective do you think the following approaches to mental health are for people?

findings.topic: trust in therapy and traditional methods
findings.finding: Far lower belief than other segments in talking therapy, medication, support groups and talking to friends and family (net efficacy well below other six segments; chart unlabelled).
findings.wording: Net efficacy (effective minus ineffective)

findings.finding: Openness to digital: more likely than the public to rate AI-based therapy effective, and higher awareness of new tech; no more sceptical than average on VR or spiritual practices.
findings.value: 31% say AI-based therapy could be effective (public 21%)

findings.finding: Criticise one-size-fits-all support; want bespoke and culturally diverse approaches.
Lowest support for early intervention of any segment, though still about three quarters.
findings.wording: Providing support at an early stage should be the main focus vs focusing on serious pre-existing conditions

findings.finding: Exceptionally low trust in every institutional voice; only the NHS, universities and people with lived experience get net positive trust. Even personal testimony can be doubted for authenticity.
findings.wording: To what extent, if at all, do you trust each of the following to provide accurate information about mental health to the public?

findings.finding: By far the most online segment and least likely to use TV; most likely to use streaming services; biggest gamers; less likely than average to read.
findings.value: TV a top source for 38% (vs 78% of Rooted Patriots)

findings.finding: Limited appetite for more; plurality happy with current level.
findings.value: 18% want less; 19% want more

findings.finding: Most moved by wider practical benefit (shorter waits, less strain on services), far more than lived experience or clinical evidence; ideally voiced by an ordinary person rather than an institution.
findings.wording: RCT split-sample on support for pharmaceutical treatment

findings.finding: Healthcare professionals or people with lived experience; channels TV/film, social media, especially authentic influencers.

findings.value: 33% say scientific and technological advances will have little or no impact

findings.finding: Distinct distrust of national and local government; also, like Progressive Activists, uneasy about the profit motive in research.

findings.finding: Strongly back in-person therapy but much less so online therapy; tied with Dissenting Disruptors as most likely to feel 'very uncomfortable' talking to a therapist online.
findings.value: in-person therapy effective 80%; online therapy effective 59%
findings.wording: How effective or ineffective do you think the following approaches to mental health are for people?

findings.finding: Low awareness of digital interventions and more undecided than opposed, except AI chatbots which they distrust; second only to Traditional Conservatives in discomfort with AI chatbots, wearables and VR.
findings.value: mobile apps: 34% effective, 30% ineffective, 36% don't know

findings.finding: TV is essential; soap operas (EastEnders, Coronation Street) are a key frame of reference for mental health. The report prints 78% (TV as a top information source) and 77% (TV news).
findings.value: TV 78% top source (p27); TV news 77% vs social media 27% (p69)

findings.finding: More open than other socially conservative segments to mental health on screen; plurality say current level is right.
findings.value: 15% want less; 42% right; 27% want more

findings.finding: Prefer everyday people with lived experience over celebrities or paid actors; NHS frontline voices over institutional ones; channel TV/film.

findings.finding: Seven in ten would be comfortable if a friend opened up.

findings.finding: 'Snowflake' views are a minority even here: about a third think people often use mental health as an excuse.
